passage: Kavitha from the second floor was in the colony sandpit again this evening. I was on the bench with my book. Three kids had their own things going: one digging a hole, one filling cups, Kavitha making a "cake" with leaves. She handed the boy her spade and took his cup, chatting about her cake the whole time. He talked about his hole. Nobody built anything together, but they looked happy. — Lalit, neighbour

qa.q: What was Kavitha making in the sandpit?
qa.a: She was making a "cake" with leaves.

qa.q: What seems to have been Kavitha's mood while swapping toys and chatting?
qa.a: She looked happy and interested; Lalit only saw her from the bench, so he can guess at her mood but not know it for sure.

qa.q: How could an adult nearby support this kind of play?
qa.a: Offer enough spades and cups to go round and let the children chat and swap freely without forcing one shared project.

qa.q: How might the boy digging the hole experience playing near Kavitha?
qa.a: He gets company and a spade to use while still doing his own digging, which feels friendly without pressure.

grounding: A neighbour notices children sharing toys and talking in a sandpit while each pursues a separate project.

passage:
Monday: At the play table, Afreen and Bidisha rolled playdough side by side. Neither spoke. Afreen kept the star cutter close to her chest.
Wednesday: Bidisha pointed. "Can I have the star?" Afreen passed it over. "I'm making biscuits," she said. "I'm making a snake," said Bidisha.
The next Monday: They chattered nonstop, swapping cutters back and forth, Afreen with her biscuits and Bidisha with a whole snake family, each admiring the other's.

qa.q: What was Afreen making on Wednesday?
qa.a: She said she was making biscuits.

qa.q: What does Afreen holding the star cutter close on Monday suggest?
qa.a: She may have felt protective of it and not yet ready to share with Bidisha.

qa.q: How could a teacher gently encourage this change?
qa.a: Place the girls near each other with a few shared tools, so asking and swapping happen naturally.

qa.q: How is the play different for Bidisha by the next Monday?
qa.a: She now has a chatty partner who swaps cutters with her, even though they are still making different things.

grounding: Over days two girls move from silent side-by-side play to sharing and talking while each keeps her own creation.

passage: The power went out just as the rain began, and Farida's small front room grew dim and crowded. Arohi and Farida lay on the floor near the window with one tin of crayons between them. Arohi drew a rainbow, Farida a house. "Pass the blue?" "Here. My sky needs it too." They swapped, chattering about their own pictures while the rain drummed. When Farida's cousin squeezed in, they pushed the tin toward him.

qa.q: How many tins of crayons did Arohi and Farida have?
qa.a: They had one tin of crayons between them.

qa.q: Why do you think the girls kept talking while they drew?
qa.a: They seemed to enjoy each other's company and wanted to share what they were making, even with different pictures.

qa.q: What helped the girls cope with the power cut?
qa.a: Moving close to the window for light and sharing the one tin let them keep playing happily.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel when they push the tin toward him?
qa.a: He would probably feel welcome to join, even without being part of a shared plan. 🙂

grounding: During a power cut, two children share crayons and chat, each drawing their own picture.

passage: In the colony park sandpit in Chennai, Ishita was patting a sand 'cake'. Zainab plopped down beside her with a bucket. 'Can I have your spade?' Ishita handed it over and took Zainab's rake. 'My cake has candles,' Ishita said, sticking in twigs. 'I'm making a well,' said Zainab, digging deep. They chatted about Ishita's cat and Zainab's new shoes, swapping tools, but neither touched the other's sand.

qa.q: What was Zainab making in the sand?
qa.a: She was making a well, digging deep.

qa.q: What does their easy swapping of tools suggest about how the girls felt?
qa.a: It suggests they felt friendly and comfortable together, happy to share while each enjoyed her own project.

qa.q: How could a parent nearby support this kind of play?
qa.a: They could let it flow and perhaps offer an extra bucket, without pushing the girls to build one thing together.

qa.q: What would change if Zainab had tried to add her well to Ishita's cake?
qa.a: The play would become shared, and they might need to agree on a plan or might argue over it.

grounding: Illustrates children playing side by side, sharing and chatting, without a single shared goal.

passage:
"Aditi, can I use purple?" Francis asked.
"Okay. Give me green."
"I'm making a dragon."
"I'm making my Ammamma's house."
"My dragon eats clouds."
"My house has a mango tree." Aditi scribbled green leaves.
"Ooh, give me purple back."
"Wait, I'm doing flowers."
"Okay." Francis waited, humming. "Your tree is big."
"Your dragon is funny," Aditi giggled.

qa.q: What was Francis drawing?
qa.a: Francis was drawing a dragon that eats clouds.

qa.q: How can you tell Francis felt patient about the purple crayon?
qa.a: Francis stayed calm, saying 'Okay' and waiting, humming, instead of grabbing it back.

qa.q: What could an adult do to support this kind of play?
qa.a: They could provide enough crayons and let the children chat, praising their kindness in swapping without forcing a joint drawing.

qa.q: What might Aditi feel when Francis says the tree is big?
qa.a: Aditi probably feels pleased and noticed, which is why Aditi giggles and compliments the dragon back. 😊

grounding: Shows children sharing materials and talking while each works on a separate drawing.

passage:
Teacher's note, Nirmala, sand corner
Leela (5) and three others were at the sand tray for twenty minutes. Each made something different: Leela a "cake", the boy beside her a road. They chatted the whole time, "Mine has candles," "Mine has a truck," and swapped spades twice. When Leela needed the sieve, she asked for it and got it. Nobody tried to make one thing together. Tomorrow I'll put out one big tray and see what happens 🙂

qa.q: How long were the children at the sand tray?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Leela have felt while chatting beside the others?
qa.a: She seemed happy and interested, enjoying the company while making her own cake.

qa.q: Why is Nirmala's one-big-tray idea a sensible next step?
qa.a: It gently invites the children to share space and maybe a shared idea, without forcing them.

qa.q: How might the boy making the road see his time at the sand tray?
qa.a: He probably enjoyed having someone to talk to and swap spades with while still doing his own thing.

grounding: Shows children playing side by side, talking and sharing tools, each on their own project, noted by a teacher.

passage: Behind the temple in their small town, Usha and Minakshi, both five, sat in the wet clay by the pond. Usha was making tiny pots. Minakshi was making snakes. "Mine is for water," Usha said. "Mine is a king snake," said Minakshi. When Usha's clay got dry, Minakshi pushed the water tin towards her without being asked. They didn't make anything together; they just kept talking, each with her own lump, until the aarti bell rang.

qa.q: What was Usha making?
qa.a: Tiny pots.

qa.q: What does Minakshi pushing the water tin towards Usha suggest?
qa.a: She felt friendly and caring towards Usha, happy to share even though they weren't working together.

qa.q: How could an adult nearby support this kind of play?
qa.a: Give them space and enough clay and water, and let them chat without insisting they build one thing together.

qa.q: How might Usha feel about playing with Minakshi?
qa.a: She likely feels comfortable and content, enjoying company without having to agree on one plan.

grounding: Shows two young girls playing side by side in clay, talking and sharing water without a shared goal.

passage: On a warm Saturday in a Toronto park, Abebe, five, was drawing a rocket in chalk on the path, his tongue between his teeth. Jin, who lived in the same building, knelt a metre away and drew a very large cat. "My rocket goes to the moon," said Abebe. "My cat eats fish," said Jin. They traded the blue chalk for the yellow, then traded back. When Jin's cat's tail reached Abebe's rocket, neither minded. They each kept drawing their own picture.

qa.q: What was Jin drawing?
qa.a: A very large cat.

qa.q: What might Abebe have felt when Jin's cat's tail reached his rocket?
qa.a: He seemed relaxed and content, not bothered, because they were happy playing side by side.

qa.q: What could a parent do to extend this play?
qa.a: Offer more chalk and ask each child about their picture, without pushing them to join the drawings.

qa.q: What would change if one child wanted to make a single big picture together?
qa.a: They would need to agree on a plan, turning it into a different, more cooperative kind of play.

grounding: Shows two young children drawing side by side, chatting and swapping chalk, each on their own picture.

passage: At the anganwadi in Bhopal, Raghav and Tanvir, both five, sat at the same clay table. Raghav was making a snake. Tanvir was making a roti. "Give me the blue roller," Tanvir said. Raghav passed it without looking. "My snake is longer than the table." "My roti is for my Nani." "Can I have the red clay?" "Take." They chatted the whole time, swapping tools, but neither asked what the other was making. When the bell rang, a long snake lay next to a lumpy roti.

qa.q: What was Raghav making?
qa.a: A snake.

qa.q: How was Raghav feeling while passing the roller without looking?
qa.a: Raghav felt absorbed and content, happy to share while busy with his snake.

qa.q: How could the anganwadi worker gently build on this play?
qa.a: The worker could suggest a small shared idea, like the snake visiting Nani's kitchen, without forcing it.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Raghav at the clay table?
qa.a: Tanvir probably sees him as a friendly table-mate who shares tools, even though they make different things.

grounding: At an anganwadi, two five-year-olds share clay tools and chat while each makes his own thing.

passage: I'm Pankaj, Jatin's cousin. In the Christmas holidays we went to Calangute beach, and Jatin, five, started digging next to a girl he'd never met. She had a pink spade; he had a yellow bucket. They talked non-stop. "Mine is a castle." "Mine is a swimming pool." "Can I use your spade?" "Only one time." They swapped buckets and spades and poured water into each other's holes, but each kept building their own thing. When her family left, Jatin waved and went on digging.

qa.q: What colour was the girl's spade?
qa.a: Pink.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling as he dug and talked?
qa.a: Jatin seemed happy and absorbed, enjoying company while building his own castle.

qa.q: How could Pankaj help Jatin try more cooperative play next time?
qa.a: Pankaj could suggest joining the castle and pool into one project and help plan it together.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see the two children playing?
qa.a: Pankaj notices they share and chat a lot but each builds their own thing, side by side with conversation.

grounding: A cousin describes a five-year-old sharing tools and chatting with a stranger at the beach while each builds separately.

passage:
First cold week of December. At the Darjeeling kindergarten, Urmila and Dolma, both four, sit at the easels side by side. They share one pot of water and chat, but Urmila paints snow and Dolma paints her dog.
A week later. They swap colours without asking, and Dolma says, "Your snow is like my dog's fur."
Just before the winter break. Dolma paints a tiny dog on Urmila's snow, and Urmila adds a red sun to her friend's picture. Both laugh.

qa.q: What did Urmila paint in the first week?
qa.a: Snow.

qa.q: What might Urmila have felt when Dolma painted a dog on her snow?
qa.a: Urmila probably felt surprised and pleased, joining in with a red sun and laughing.

qa.q: How could the teacher encourage this growing play?
qa.a: Keep the easels side by side, provide shared materials, and let them discover joint painting on their own.

qa.q: How might Dolma see Urmila by the winter break?
qa.a: Dolma seems to see Urmila as a friend to share with, comfortable enough to paint on her picture.

grounding: Over a winter month, two four-year-olds move from painting side by side to adding to each other's pictures.

passage:
The rain wouldn't stop, and the power went out in the Amritsar flat. Gurleen and Darshan, both five, sat by the window with one box of crayons between them.

"I'm drawing a cow," Gurleen said.

"I'm drawing a car. Pass the blue."

She passed it. "My cow is eating."

"My car is going fast."

They drew side by side, chatting, sharing crayons, each busy with their own picture, until the lights came back.

qa.q: What was Gurleen drawing?
qa.a: Gurleen was drawing a cow.

qa.q: How did the children seem to feel during the power cut?
qa.a: They seemed content and busy, happily chatting while they drew.

qa.q: How could an adult support this kind of play?
qa.a: Give them shared materials, like one box of crayons, and let them chat and draw side by side.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel when Gurleen passed him the blue?
qa.a: Darshan would feel pleased and included, able to keep drawing his car.

grounding: During a rainy power cut, two children share crayons and chat while each draws their own picture.

passage:
After Dussehra, the colony park in Jaipur had a fresh pile of sand. Farida and Irawati, both four, sat next to each other with one bucket and two spoons.

Farida was making a hill. Irawati was digging a hole.

"Can I have the bucket?" Irawati asked.

"After me," Farida said, and handed it over a moment later.

They chatted about their dolls while working. Farida's hill and Irawati's hole never met.

qa.q: What was Farida making?
qa.a: Farida was making a hill.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Farida handed over the bucket?
qa.a: Irawati was pleased and happy to get the bucket.

qa.q: How could a parent encourage Farida and Irawati to play together more?
qa.a: Suggest a small shared idea, like making a hill with a hole for water, without forcing it.

qa.q: How might Farida see sharing the bucket?
qa.a: Farida seemed to see it as fine after a first turn, handing it over a moment later.

grounding: After Dussehra, two children play side by side in the sand, sharing a bucket and chatting without a shared goal.

passage:
Rainy-day note, Aizawl nursery, July
With the playground flooded, Vishal and Lalremsiami spent the morning at the sand tray. They shared the spades and the red bucket and chatted the whole time. Vishal was building "a big road for trucks"; Lalremsiami was making "cakes for my mama's birthday". Each told the other about their project, but neither joined in. When Vishal needed the bucket, he asked and she handed it over. Tomorrow I'll add a second bucket and see if a shared idea grows.
Ms Zohmingthangi

qa.q: What was Vishal building in the sand tray?
qa.a: He was building "a big road for trucks".

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami seem to feel while making her cakes?
qa.a: She seemed happy and absorbed in her own project, content to chat and share without joining Vishal's road.

qa.q: How could Ms Zohmingthangi gently encourage a shared goal?
qa.a: She could suggest a link, like trucks delivering the cakes, and let the children decide whether to join up.

qa.q: What would change if the two had one shared plan?
qa.a: They would need to agree on what they were making, so their chatting would turn into planning and taking turns.

grounding: Shows two young children sharing tools and talking during rainy-season play while each works on a separate idea.
